newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mbeki reiterates privatisation policy.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mbeki reiterates privatisation policy.

text.p: The privatisation of state assets should never be done at the expense of the voiceless in South Africa, deputy president Thabo Mbeki told National Union of Metalworkers (Numsa) delegates on Wednesday.

Addressing the 232,000 strong union at its triannual congress in Johannesburg, Mbeki said the government would never act in a way that would hamper its ability to change for the better the lives of South Africans.
"But you cannot sit and say here are state assets, business as usual...it cannot be business as usual," he said.
State assets had been built to serve particular interests during the apartheid era and had to be restructured to provide better service to people who had been denied in the past.

"We have talked about the restructuring of state assets so that we can restructure state assets in defence of the interests of the voiceless," Mbeki told delegates attending the five-day congress -- the first since South Africa's first democratic elections more than two years ago.
"The first and most important point is that we have to expand the telecommunications sector radically," he added.

"As a consequence, Telkom will be too small to handle an expanded telecommunications infrastructure. Government does not have money to invest in an expanded telecommunications sector and therefore we are saying let's take part of Telkom and look for foreign investors."
The government would maintain majority ownership to ensure that the expanded telecommunications sector provided more and better service to people who were denied service before.
Numsa national president Mtutuzeli Tom said the union faced a number of "hard choices" among them privatisation.
Other challenges were competitiveness, globalisation and downsizing in the metal industry.

"It's important for Numsa to understand the environment in which we operate. We are no longer fighting against government, but must ensure that government delivers to our interest and needs," Mtutuzeli said.
A crucial problem facing the union was "the rising degree of hopelessness and confusion of members" and increasing gap between shop stewards and members.
Some of the key issues to be debated at the congress, which ends on Sunday, include economic policy, the privatisation of state assets and collective bargaining.
